claims.text: The starting composite contains tungsten particles or interconnected tungsten ligaments embedded in a copper matrix.
The untreated W–Cu composite exhibits phase separation and interfacial voids.
The intervention is deposition of a sub-micron Ti/Ni alloy coating on tungsten by a method such as magnetron sputtering before consolidation.
Magnetron-sputtered Ti/Ni coatings can be combined with spark plasma sintering to produce a coated-particle composite.
During consolidation, the Ti/Ni coating will react with both tungsten and copper.
The coating-induced reactions will create a graded interfacial transition layer in W–Cu.
The transition layer will reduce W–Cu interfacial energy.
The Ti/Ni coating will improve wettability and chemical bonding at the W–Cu interface.
Improved interfacial bonding will minimize voids and phase-separated regions in the W–Cu composite.
The reactive coating will form an intermetallic or amorphous transition layer between tungsten and copper.
A graded interface will reduce mismatch stresses and promote atomic matching.
Reduced dewetting and void formation will improve thermal transport through the composite.
The coated W–Cu composite will have significantly higher thermal conductivity than an otherwise identical untreated composite.
The coated interface will resist degradation under irradiation and thermal cycling better than the untreated interface.
Poor W–Cu adhesion causes phase separation and void formation under high thermal and irradiation loads.
The proposed treatment is applicable under service conditions representative of joints between tungsten plasma-facing components and copper-based cooling systems.
In an HEA/diamond composite, magnetron-sputtered Ti/Ni coating followed by spark plasma sintering produced better interfacial bonding than in the uncoated composite.
CoCrFeNi/Al calculations predicted a stable three-dimensional transition layer with little mismatch stress and strong chemical bonding.
